title: New malware doesn’t call home, it turns your Exchange server into its home
summary: There’s a new flavor of cereal on the table, but not the appealing kind, particularly for defenders. A new report from global security company ESET describes a “sophisticated, modular, and tightly interconnected” toolset designed to run on compromised Exchange servers for long-term cyberespionage. The malware is named ‘Cereal’ because it relies heavily on serialization, a technique used to package data and code for transport. It comprises a novel Exchange email collection module, a sneaky command and control (C&C) mechanism, and clever .NET execution tricks. While as of now, it is being used by nation-state actors to attack government bodies , enterprises should still be concerned. “Tradecraft like this tends not to stay with its inventors,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, citing a baseball analogy: “Criminal groups study nation-state techniques the way minor leaguers study a big league pitcher’s grip. What works in the majors eventually shows up in every ballpark.” Sophisticated tradecraft ESET describes Cereal as a malware toolkit that runs on Microsoft Exchange servers, receives commands and executes them in memory, maps the victim organization, and collects selected email messages. No external network infrastructure was identified; instead, the toolkit contains a passive backdoor that runs on targeted servers and provides access. It leaves little on disk. The researchers noted that one of the most interesting aspects of the toolkit is what they did not find: External C&C infrastructure. The victim’s compromised Exchange server is effectively “co-opted” to play the part. Operators send commands as separate, but similarly-structured, executables, suggesting an automated framework.
